shortlist.raw_text: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.

shortlist.raw_text: Vision-language-action models are typically built on a simple premise: perception is first compressed by visual encoders, and action reasoning begins only afterwards. Yet manipulation often hinges on precisely the visual signals most vulnerable to this abstraction, e.g., local geometry, boundaries, depth, and subtle state changes. This raises a fundamental question: should action policies inherit a fixed visual endpoint, or directly access evolving visual computation? We introduce NEO-VLA, a structurally encoder-free vision-language-action framework. Images are tokenized by lightweight patch convolutional layers and evolve jointly with language throughout the backbone, allowing a flow-matching action expert to draw from instruction-conditioned visual representations at different depths. This simple change reveals a consistent pattern. Native architectures outperform encoder-based counterparts under controlled comparisons; full fine-tuning reduces but does not erase the gap, and additional scale alone cannot recover it. More strikingly, layer-wise probing shows that the action-critical signals often peak well before the final visual representation. Across diverse manipulation settings and distribution shifts, NEO-VLA consequently achieves stronger and more robust control. Together, these results suggest that embodied control benefits from access to visual representations across the computational hierarchy, rather than a fixed encoder output.

shortlist.raw_text: Computer graphics is built on code. Large language model (LLM) agents can now generate graphics code and iteratively refine it through various feedback. This capability opens the door to a potentially new paradigm of computer graphics, with graphics algorithms increasingly built around agentic systems to automate progressively complex tasks. Over the past years, research on agentic graphics has expanded rapidly across a diverse range of tasks. This rapid growth makes it increasingly difficult for manual literature reviews to keep pace with new developments. At the same time, similar ideas are often described using different terminology across these tasks, further complicating efforts to develop a systematic understanding of the field. In this report, we address these challenges through two contributions. First, we introduce a unified taxonomy for characterizing agentic systems across diverse computer graphics tasks. Second, we develop an agentic literature system that can assist human researchers in analyzing existing and newly published papers at scale. Building on these contributions, we analyze emerging research trends and discuss open challenges in coordinating agents and tools across graphics tasks, designing interfaces and representations for human-agent collaboration, sustaining long-horizon planning and refinement, and reliably evaluating interactive graphics systems.

Just how private are the conversations you have with your favorite AI? Last week, news broke that conversations from Anthropic’s Claude AI could be accessed through a Google dork (translation: advanced search query). Yes, people had already shared these conversations with others via active links. But I’m sure they never imagined that the topics discussed could be exposed to anyone with some search savvy. Also: 5 reasons you should be more tight-lipped with your chatbot Anthropic quickly fixed the “exploit” to disable this type of indexing. But the question remains: Just how private are your AI conversations? In part, that depends on you. Though the AI companies don’t always make it easy, they do offer controls through which you’re able to manage your own privacy. Toward that end, let’s look at four major AI chatbots and cover steps to tighten your privacy as much as possible. Don’t want your conversations in ChatGPT tracked or saved? You can chat with the AI without an account. Even if you have one, just log out before you submit your query. Certain advanced features won’t be available, and you’ll hit lower thresholds. But if you don’t want to expose specific conversations, this is certainly an option. If you are signed in with your account and don’t want your next chat saved to your history, make it a temporary one. At the ChatGPT window, click the circular “Turn on Temporary Chat” icon in the upper right. The prompt field will turn black while a notice tells you how it works. You still may not want to share anything too sensitive. But at least you can discuss more personal topics since the chatbot won’t remember any of it. Also: Microsoft’s new Copilot app puts everything in one place – but the price is ‘evolving’ OpenAI trains its ChatGPT model in part based on your conversations. Though the shared data isn’t associated with your name and account, you might still want to turn off this option to prevent any personal information from being shared. Click your account name at the bottom of the left pane. Select Settings and go to Data controls. If the option for “Improve the model for everyone” is turned on, click it and turn it off. Also: Claude’s Record-a-Skill cut my research from hours to 30 minutes – but the magic has limits ChatGPT gives you the ability to share a conversation via X, LinkedIn, Reddit, or through a regular link. But as long as your conversation exists, that link remains active. Users can block future data harvesting by adjusting account toggles on ChatGPT, Gemini, and LinkedIn, or by submitting formal objection forms through Meta’s Privacy Center. Every time you type a prompt into ChatGPT , search with Gemini , or share a post on Instagram, big tech companies harvest your data to train their artificial intelligence models. Major platforms like LinkedIn and Gemini turn training settings on by default, while OpenAI and Meta quietly use public posts, photos, and chat logs unless you explicitly object. As NotebookCheck highlights, taking back control of your privacy takes about fifteen minutes, but you need to know where to look. Here is how to disable data harvesting across the biggest platforms on the web. OpenAI makes toggling off training relatively straightforward in ChatGPT. Head into your account settings, open the Data Controls tab, and switch off “Improve the model for everyone.” You can also request a permanent opt-out through OpenAI’s privacy portal . Keep in mind that if you rate a response with a thumbs up or down, that specific conversation bypasses your privacy preferences. For extra sensitive questions, stick to temporary chats. Google bundles its AI controls under “Keep Activity” on the Gemini web interface and app. Opening your activity settings lets you turn off future data collection or wipe your chat history entirely. However, Google keeps unlinked conversation logs for up to 72 hours for safety reviews. Plus, any chats previously analyzed by human reviewers remain stored for up to three years. Meta skips simple toggles entirely, requiring users to fill out formal objection forms hidden inside its Privacy Center . A separate form exists for WhatsApp, though Meta states it currently refrains from training on WhatsApp AI chats. LinkedIn quietly enabled EU data training for generative AI models under its “Data for Generative AI Improvement” privacy setting. text:
Personal subscribers to Google AI might assume a paid tier shields their data. 

Gemini's terms show that paying a subscription fee does not remove your conversations from the training pipeline.

If you use a personal Google AI subscription, every saved chat can be fed back into model training. You cannot turn off training while preserving your saved history. Your only options are disabling chat history entirely or using temporary chat sessions.

The policy extends beyond automated training:
Unlinked conversation logs are retained for up to 72 hours for safety reviews. Human reviewers can read saved chat transcripts, and chats analyzed by humans remain stored for up to 3 years. That is why Google's support page explicitly warns users not to enter confidential information.

Disconnecting reviewed chats from your account removes your identity, but the raw text stays on Google's servers. 

This policy applies specifically to personal subscriber accounts. Corporate enterprise tiers operate under separate agreements with strict data boundaries, but consumer tiers leave your inputs in the pool.

Source: Hacker News, with reporting from note and ZDNet

*Line 2:* Personal account subscribers have no direct toggle to opt out of training without deleting their saved history.
*When to prefer:* Use when addressing tech-forward readers who already use Gemini daily and assume paid tiers grant standard data privacy.

Your paid Google AI subscription does not buy you conversation privacy.
*Line 2:* Saved Gemini chats are used for model training by default, and human reviewers may read the transcripts.
*When to prefer:* Use for general professionals and founders who pay for consumer AI tools out of pocket and expect consumer protection in return.
